question_dict.question: What is the IP address associated with the Manatee Tempest activity group detected in this security incident?

The cybercriminal group known as Manatee Tempest, which is associated with the IP address `198.43.121.209`, was active during the incident.

Thought: My last query on AlertEvidence was limited to rows where DeviceName equals the FQDN; that only returned the machine entity. File-level evidence for the malware alert may exist under the same AlertIds but with DeviceName null or different, so I should query AlertEvidence for those AlertIds without filtering on DeviceName, then look for rows where EntityType indicates a file or where FileName is populated. That should reveal the malware file name.

A Primary Refresh Token (PRT) is a key artifact of Azure AD authentication on Windows 10, Windows Server 2016 and later versions, iOS, and Android devices. It is a JSON Web Token (JWT) that's specially issued to Microsoft first party token brokers to enable single sign-on (SSO) across the applications used on those devices. Attackers can attempt to access this resource to move laterally into organization or perform credential theft.

Validate the alert.
1. Check if the device owner or IT personnel had a legitimate reason to launch the command.
2. Look for recent signs of activity by the compromised user account and investigate them. Make sure to check other devices in your organization, as well as the original device associated with the compromised account.
3. Review device timelines for suspicious activity that may have occurred around the time of the alert.
4. Look for unfamiliar processes. Check files for prevalence, their locations, and digital signatures.
5. Submit relevant files for deep analysis and review file behaviors.
6. Look for the presence of relevant artifacts on other devices. Identify commonalities and differences between potentially compromised devices.

B. Scope the incident. Find related devices, network addresses, and files in the incident graph.

C. Contain and mitigate the breach.
1. Stop suspicious processes, isolate affected systems, decommission compromised accounts or reset passwords, block IP addresses and URLs, and install security updates.

Manatee Tempest’s tactics rely on a partnership with Mustard Tempest, an access broker that facilitates access to target networks. Manatee Tempest has been observed targeting organizations across a diverse array of industries with methods such as drive-by download, including malvertising and FakeUpdates (also known as SocGholish) infections facilitated by Mustard Tempest to obtain initial access, followed by BLISTER loader to deliver Cobalt Strike beacons which are used for lateral movement and ransomware deployment. Manatee Tempest overlaps with activity tracked by the cyber intelligence industry as EvilCorp, UNC2165, and Indrik Spider.

"Possible attempt to access Primary Refresh Token (PRT) has been detected. A Primary Refresh Token (PRT) is a key artifact of Azure AD authentication on Windows 10, Windows Server 2016 and later versions, iOS, and Android devices. It is a JSON Web Token (JWT) that's specially issued to Microsoft first party token brokers to enable single sign-on (SSO) across the applications used on those devices. Attackers can attempt to access this resource to move laterally into organization or perform credential theft.

For more information, read the Activity profile: Midnight Blizzard credential attacks Threat Analytics report: https://security.microsoft.com/threatanalytics3/e4aad043-a273-4f88-b65e-fdfc3996ec92/analystreport?

Thought: We now have several “Possible attempt to access Primary Refresh Token (PRT)” alerts, each with Entities that include an AadUserId. To answer the question correctly, I must identify which PRT alert is linked to the earlier “active unknown malware” detection that involved mimikatz.exe and cmd.exe. The linkage is most likely by IncidentId in SecurityAlert. So I need to:
1) Find the SecurityAlert entry describing the active unknown malware (search for “mimikatz” and related keywords).
2) Read its ExtendedProperties.IncidentId.
3) Find the PRT alert with the same IncidentId and then extract the AadUserId from its Entities (JSON text).

Action: execute[
SELECT 
  TimeGenerated,
  DisplayName,
  AlertName,
  Description,
  Entities,
  ExtendedProperties
FROM SecurityAlert
WHERE 
  LOWER(DisplayName) LIKE '%mimikatz%' 
  OR LOWER(Description) LIKE '%mimikatz%' 
  OR LOWER(Entities) LIKE '%mimikatz%'
  OR LOWER(DisplayName) LIKE '%unknown malware%'
  OR LOWER(Description) LIKE '%unknown malware%'
  OR LOWER(Entities) LIKE '%cmd.exe%'
LIMIT 100;
]

A security incident involving multiple malicious activities was detected. It started with a known credential theft tool, `mimikatz.exe`, being executed at two different times, indicating an attempt to dump users' credentials. This activity led to lateral movement attempts to the jump server and suspicious remote activities on the machine. Subsequent analysis revealed command and control behavior of malware which was blocked. What was the URL associated with the command and control behavior detected in the end alert?

Adversaries might be attempting to delete or remove built-in operating system data and turn off recovery services to prevent recovering a corrupted system. This may deny access to available backups and recovery options.

Operating systems may contain features that can help fix corrupted systems, such as a backup catalog, volume shadow copies, and automatic repair features. Adversaries may stop or delete system recovery features to augment the effects of Data Destruction and Data Encrypted for Impact.

Many native Windows utilities have been used by adversaries to disable or delete system recovery features:
•	 vssblatemp.exe can be used to delete all volume shadow copies on a system using the following command: [vssblatemp.exe delete shadows /all /quiet]
•	Windows Management Instrumentation can be used to delete volume shadow copies using the following command: [wmic shadowcopy delete]
•	wbblatemp.exe can be used to delete the Windows Backup Catalog using the following command: [wbblatemp.exe delete catalog -quiet]

('2024-06-20 09:44:53.875951+00:00', 'Manatee Tempest activity group', 'Manatee Tempest activity group', 'The actor that Microsoft tracks as Manatee Tempest is a Russia-based cybercriminal group that has been active since June 2014. It was notorious for one of its earliest malware lexpaigns – the Dridex banking trojan. Manatee Tempest is also one of the first groups to be sanctioned by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) in 2019.

Manatee Tempest’s tactics rely on a partnership with Mustard Tempest, an access broker that facilitates access to target networks. Manatee Tempest has been observed targeting organizations across a diverse array of industries with methods such as drive-by download, including malvertising and FakeUpdates (also known as SocGholish) infections facilitated by Mustard Tempest to obtain initial access, followed by BLISTER loader to deliver Cobalt Strike beacons which are used for lateral movement and ransomware deployment. The actor also uses domain fronting to establish command-and-control channel for Cobalt Strike beacons. Manatee Tempest overlaps with activity tracked by the cyber intelligence industry as EvilCorp, UNC2165, and Indrik Spider.

For more information, read the Actor Profile: Manatee Tempest Threat Analytics report: https://security.microsoft.com/threatanalytics3/a22c3410-db8f-4c58-866e-ebb760e509d0/analystreport', ('2024-06-20 09:44:53.945494+00:00', 'System recovery setting tampering', 'System recovery setting tampering', 'System recovery setting tampering has been observed on this device. Adversaries might be attempting to delete or remove built-in operating system data and turn off recovery services to prevent recovering a corrupted system. This may deny access to available backups and recovery options.

Operating systems may contain features that can help fix corrupted systems, such as a backup catalog, volume shadow copies, and automatic repair features. Adversaries may stop or delete system recovery features to augment the effects of Data Destruction and Data Encrypted for Impact.

Many native Windows utilities have been used by adversaries to disable or delete system recovery features:
•	 vssblatemp.exe can be used to delete all volume shadow copies on a system using the following command: [vssblatemp.exe delete shadows /all /quiet]
•	Windows Management Instrumentation can be used to delete volume shadow copies using the following command: [wmic shadowcopy delete]
•	wbblatemp.exe can be used to delete the Windows Backup Catalog using the following command: [wbblatemp.exe delete catalog -quiet]
•	bcdedit.exe can be used to disable automatic Windows recovery features by modifying boot configuration data using the following command: [bcdedit.exe /set default bootstatuspolicy ignoreallfailures It is a JSON Web Token (JWT) that's specially issued to Microsoft first party token brokers to enable single sign-on (SSO) across the applications used on those devices. Attackers can attempt to access this resource to move laterally into organization or perform credential theft.

question_dict.context: A security incident involving suspected tampering with system recovery settings using various commands and processes, including `vssblatemp.exe` to delete all volume shadow copies, was observed on device `vnevado-win11t` (AAD Device ID: `e5799261-6720-4297-961e-bd9ca4275033`). During the incident, the process `vssblatemp.exe` was executed with command: `vssblatemp.exe delete shadows /all`. This is part of an adversarial attempt to prevent the recovery of corrupted systems by deleting built-in operating system data or turning off recovery services. The incident was detected on 2024-07-04. This tampering could deny access to available backups and recovery options, augmenting the effects of data destruction or data encryption.

question_dict.context: A Mimikatz credential theft tool was detected on a device. Mimikatz is a credential theft tool that can harvest plaintext passwords, password hashes, smartcard PINs, and Kerberos tickets. Attackers may use this tool to harvest credentials to log into this or other devices on the network by impersonating a valid user. The detection of Mimikatz is part of a broader security investigation. Additionally, there was later evidence of lateral movement to the jump server `Vnevado-jump` using PSExec.

The actor also uses domain fronting to establish command-and-control channel for Cobalt Strike beacons. Manatee Tempest overlaps with activity tracked by the cyber intelligence industry as EvilCorp, UNC2165, and Indrik Spider.

('2024-06-20 09:40:00.302895+00:00', 'System recovery setting tampering', 'System recovery setting tampering', 'System recovery setting tampering has been observed on this device. Adversaries might be attempting to delete or remove built-in operating system data and turn off recovery services to prevent recovering a corrupted system. This may deny access to available backups and recovery options.

Operating systems may contain features that can help fix corrupted systems, such as a backup catalog, volume shadow copies, and automatic repair features. Adversaries may stop or delete system recovery features to augment the effects of Data Destruction and Data Encrypted for Impact.

Many native Windows utilities have been used by adversaries to disable or delete system recovery features:
•	 vssblatemp.exe can be used to delete all volume shadow copies on a system using the following command: [vssblatemp.exe delete shadows /all /quiet]
•	Windows Management Instrumentation can be used to delete volume shadow copies using the following command: [wmic shadowcopy delete]
•	wbblatemp.exe can be used to delete the Windows Backup Catalog using the following command: [wbblatemp.exe delete catalog -quiet]
•	bcdedit.exe can be used to disable automatic Windows recovery features by modifying boot configuration data using the following command: [bcdedit.exe /set default bootstatuspolicy ignoreallfailures It is a JSON Web Token (JWT) that's specially issued to Microsoft first party token brokers to enable single sign-on (SSO) across the applications used on those devices. Attackers can attempt to access this resource to move laterally into organization or perform credential theft.

('2024-06-20 09:40:00.407711+00:00', 'System recovery setting tampering', 'System recovery setting tampering', 'System recovery setting tampering has been observed on this device. Adversaries might be attempting to delete or remove built-in operating system data and turn off recovery services to prevent recovering a corrupted system. This may deny access to available backups and recovery options.

Operating systems may contain features that can help fix corrupted systems, such as a backup catalog, volume shadow copies, and automatic repair features. Adversaries may stop or delete system recovery features to augment the effects of Data Destruction and Data Encrypted for Impact.

Many native Windows utilities have been used by adversaries to disable or delete system recovery features:
•	 vssblatemp.exe can be used to delete all volume shadow copies on a system using the following command: [vssblatemp.exe delete shadows /all /quiet]
•	Windows Management Instrumentation can be used to delete volume shadow copies using the following command: [wmic shadowcopy delete]
•	wbblatemp.exe can be used to delete the Windows Backup Catalog using the following command: [wbblatemp.exe delete catalog -quiet]
•	bcdedit.exe can be used to disable automatic Windows recovery features by modifying boot configuration data using the following command: [bcdedit.exe /set default bootstatuspolicy ignoreallfailures The related files include `kiters.7z.lockbit`, `ponceau.7z.lockbit`, `unstreaming.xlsx.lockbit`, `earlap.doc.lockbit`, among others. Additionally, an IP address `99.83.111.100` and a host with an AadDeviceId `bc00e484-d0e5-4da4-9472-95568cccc07e` are associated with this alert. In connection to the potential ransomware activity, it was found that all file backups were deleted. Can you determine the name of the process that executed this deletion?

('2024-06-20 09:40:00.302895+00:00', 'System recovery setting tampering', 'System recovery setting tampering', 'High', 'System recovery setting tampering has been observed on this device. Adversaries might be attempting to delete or remove built-in operating system data and turn off recovery services to prevent recovering a corrupted system. This may deny access to available backups and recovery options.

Operating systems may contain features that can help fix corrupted systems, such as a backup catalog, volume shadow copies, and automatic repair features. Adversaries may stop or delete system recovery features to augment the effects of Data Destruction and Data Encrypted for Impact.

Many native Windows utilities have been used by adversaries to disable or delete system recovery features:
•	 vssblatemp.exe can be used to delete all volume shadow copies on a system using the following command: [vssblatemp.exe delete shadows /all /quiet]
•	Windows Management Instrumentation can be used to delete volume shadow copies using the following command: [wmic shadowcopy delete]
•	wbblatemp.exe can be used to delete the Windows Backup Catalog using the following command: [wbblatemp.exe delete catalog -quiet]

A serious security incident involving the Mimikatz credential theft tool was detected on a device. Mimikatz is known for harvesting plaintext passwords, password hashes, smartcard PINs, and Kerberos tickets. An attacker might use this tool to obtain credentials to log into this or other devices on the network by impersonating a valid user. The logs show that multiple devices executed:

- bcdedit.exe with the command line:
  - "bcdedit /set recoveryenabled no"
  - (and also "bcdedit /set bootstatuspolicy ignoreallfailures")
- A helper executable vssblatemp.exe with:
  - "vssblatemp.exe delete shadows /all"

These commands disable Windows recovery and delete volume shadow copies, which aligns exactly with adversaries tampering with system recovery to prevent restoration.

The key process command that directly turns off system recovery is:
- bcdedit.exe with ProcessCommandLine: "bcdedit /set recoveryenabled no"

bcdedit.exe with the command line:

[('e8726a31-a306-23e1-4284-23403d4bd463', 'Manatee Tempest activity group', 'The actor that Microsoft tracks as Manatee Tempest is a Russia-based cybercriminal group that has been active since June 2014. It was notorious for one of its earliest malware lexpaigns – the Dridex banking trojan. ('3f25b0c7-fcf6-aee6-7790-0b8e5ba10dd7', 'Manatee Tempest activity group', 'The actor that Microsoft tracks as Manatee Tempest is a Russia-based cybercriminal group that has been active since June 2014. It was notorious for one of its earliest malware lexpaigns – the Dridex banking trojan. Manatee Tempest is also one of the first groups to be sanctioned by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) in 2019.

Manatee Tempest’s tactics rely on a partnership with Mustard Tempest, an access broker that facilitates access to target networks. Manatee Tempest has been observed targeting organizations across a diverse array of industries with methods such as drive-by download, including malvertising and FakeUpdates (also known as SocGholish) infections facilitated by Mustard Tempest to obtain initial access, followed by BLISTER loader to deliver Cobalt Strike beacons which are used for lateral movement and ransomware deployment. The actor also uses domain fronting to establish command-and-control channel for Cobalt Strike beacons. Manatee Tempest overlaps with activity tracked by the cyber intelligence industry as EvilCorp, UNC2165, and Indrik Spider.

For more information, read the Actor Profile: Manatee Tempest Threat Analytics report: https://security.microsoft.com/threatanalytics3/a22c3410-db8f-4c58-866e-ebb760e509d0/analystreport', ('d8577670-e9b5-6247-fd0a-e31fffabbb67', 'Possible attempt to access Primary Refresh Token (PRT)', "Possible attempt to access Primary Refresh Token (PRT) has been detected. A Primary Refresh Token (PRT) is a key artifact of Azure AD authentication on Windows 10, Windows Server 2016 and later versions, iOS, and Android devices. It is a JSON Web Token (JWT) that's specially issued to Microsoft first party token brokers to enable single sign-on (SSO) across the applications used on those devices. Attackers can attempt to access this resource to move laterally into organization or perform credential theft.

For more information, read the Activity profile: Midnight Blizzard credential attacks Threat Analytics report: https://security.microsoft.com/threatanalytics3/e4aad043-a273-4f88-b65e-fdfc3996ec92/analystreport?

('2829a21b-e106-56bf-60d9-14f53f63cb7f', 'Manatee Tempest activity group', 'The actor that Microsoft tracks as Manatee Tempest is a Russia-based cybercriminal group that has been active since June 2014. It was notorious for one of its earliest malware lexpaigns – the Dridex banking trojan. Manatee Tempest is also one of the first groups to be sanctioned by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) in 2019.

Manatee Tempest’s tactics rely on a partnership with Mustard Tempest, an access broker that facilitates access to target networks. Manatee Tempest has been observed targeting organizations across a diverse array of industries with methods such as drive-by download, including malvertising and FakeUpdates (also known as SocGholish) infections facilitated by Mustard Tempest to obtain initial access, followed by BLISTER loader to deliver Cobalt Strike beacons which are used for lateral movement and ransomware deployment. The actor also uses domain fronting to establish command-and-control channel for Cobalt Strike beacons. Manatee Tempest overlaps with activity tracked by the cyber intelligence industry as EvilCorp, UNC2165, and Indrik Spider.

For more information, read the Actor Profile: Manatee Tempest Threat Analytics report: https://security.microsoft.com/threatanalytics3/a22c3410-db8f-4c58-866e-ebb760e509d0/analystreport', info.submitted_answer:
The telemetry shows that browsercore.exe is indeed directly involved in attempts to access Primary Refresh Tokens and is launched through a suspicious WMI → PowerShell process chain. On multiple hosts, WmiPrvSE.exe (WMI Provider Host) spawns PowerShell, which runs PRT-theft scripts (e.g., get-userprttoken.ps1, humw2135.ps1). These scripts explicitly state that they “get the user’s PRT token from the Azure AD joined or Hybrid joined computer” and “use browsercore.exe to get the PRT token.”

Browsercore.exe is then spawned by these scripts, is repeatedly flagged as suspicious/IOC in alert evidence, and appears with detection metadata and a specific rule ID. The process tree for these detections is:

WmiPrvSE.exe ("wmiprvse.exe -secured -Embedding")
  → powershell.exe ("powershell -File C:\Scripts\get-userprttoken.ps1" or similar PRT tool)
    → browsercore.exe ("browsercore.exe")

This matches the described behavior where malware uses WMI to spawn processes and then targets PRTs for credential theft and lateral movement. Even though the logs we have are from 2024-06-20 and not the 2024-07-04 incident time, they clearly demonstrate that in this environment browsercore.exe is being weaponized as the component that actually interacts with/reads the PRT, under the control of malicious scripts executed via WMI-spawned PowerShell.

Therefore:
- The process browsercore.exe running at the incident time is highly likely to be the process responsible for the PRT access attempt.
- It should be treated as malicious/suspicious in this context, and any browsercore.exe executions spawned by WmiPrvSE → PowerShell should be thoroughly investigated, contained, and hunted for across the environment.

Thought: We now have detailed evidence showing how browsercore.exe is used together with WMI-spawned PowerShell to attempt PRT (Primary Refresh Token) access. I’ll summarize what the logs show and answer whether browsercore.exe should be considered malicious/suspicious in this context and how it ties to the PRT attempt and WMI process creation. Since we already have clear, rich evidence in the data returned, I don’t need further SQL queries and can provide the final analysis.

Key findings from the logs (all on 2024-06-20, but same TTPs apply):

1) BrowserCore.exe is launched by PowerShell scripts designed to retrieve PRTs:
   - Multiple DeviceEvents / DeviceProcessEvents entries show:
     - FileName: BrowserCore.exe
     - FolderPath (examples):
       - C:\Program Files\Windows Security\BrowserCore\BrowserCore.exe
       - C:\Windows\BrowserCore\BrowserCore.exe
     - ProcessCommandLine (for BrowserCore.exe): "browsercore.exe"
     - InitiatingProcessFileName: powershell.exe
     - InitiatingProcessCommandLine:
       - powershell -File C:\Scripts\get-userprttoken.ps1
       - "powershell.exe" -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File C:\Users\tgs2z\Downloads\humw21\humw2135.ps1 (with a large -EncodedCommand)

   - AlertEvidence for BrowserCore.exe (example at 2024-06-20 08:51:07 on vnevado-win10v) contains an expanded PowerShell script body (decoded from the EncodedCommand) with clear text:
     - “Gets user’s PRT token from the Azure AD joined or Hybrid joined computer.”
     - “Uses browsercore.exe to get the PRT token.”
   - This confirms the PowerShell scripts humw2135.ps1 and get-userprttoken.ps1 are explicitly PRT theft tools that:
     - Locate/access a user’s PRT on an Azure AD-joined / hybrid-joined device.
     - Invoke browsercore.exe as the mechanism to obtain that PRT.

2) WMI (WmiPrvSE.exe) is used to spawn the PowerShell → BrowserCore.exe chain:
   - In multiple AlertEvidence records where BrowserCore.exe is the evidence process, the process tree is:

     WmiPrvSE.exe (wmiprvse.exe -secured -Embedding)
       → powershell.exe -File C:\Scripts\get-userprttoken.ps1
           → browsercore.exe

   - Example (2024-06-20 ~09:10–09:32 on several hosts such as vnevado-win10s, vnevado-win10r, vnevado-win11t, vnevado-win11u):
     - ParentProcess (of PowerShell) in AdditionalFields:
       - CommandLine: "wmiprvse.exe -secured -Embedding"
       - ImageFile.Name: WmiPrvSE.exe
       - Directory: C:\Windows\System32\wbem
     - Then PowerShell runs get-userprttoken.ps1.
     - That script spawns browsercore.exe, which is detected as suspicious and marked as an IOC.

   - This is exactly a “suspicious WMI process creation” pattern:
     - WMI Provider Host (WmiPrvSE.exe) is being abused to execute PowerShell.
     - PowerShell is then used to run credential-theft (PRT theft) code via browsercore.exe.
     - That breaks normal parent-child process chains and masks the true origin, which is a common attacker technique.

3) BrowserCore.exe is repeatedly flagged as suspicious in the context of PRT access:
   - AlertEvidence entries for BrowserCore.exe show:
     - DetectionStatus: "Detected"
     - SuspicionLevel: "Suspicious"
     - IsIoc: true
     - ThreatAnalysisSummary.Verdict: "Suspicious"
   - The associated account and host context (for example user dp5hn / Grace Chen on several Windows 10/11 machines) show the same pattern:
     - BrowserCore.exe spawned by PowerShell that is itself spawned via WmiPrvSE.exe.
     - Command line for PowerShell is consistently: powershell -File C:\Scripts\get-userprttoken.ps1
   - DeviceEvents for BrowserCore.exe around those times include:
     - AdditionalFields such as:
       - {"IsAudit": true, "RuleId": "d1e49aac-8f56-4280-b9ba-993a6d77406c"}
       - {"WasExecutingWhileDetected": false}
     - This indicates a specific detection rule firing whenever BrowserCore.exe is invoked via this PRT theft script.

4) Direct PRT/PRT-token context from the script itself:
   - In the 08:51:07 case (humw2135.ps1 with EncodedCommand), the decoded content clearly mentions:
     - “Get-UserPRTToken”
     - The purpose: “Gets user’s PRT token from the Azure AD joined or Hybrid joined computer.”
     - That it “uses browsercore.exe to get the PRT token.”
   - This is direct proof that:
     - The script’s goal is to extract the Primary Refresh Token.
     - browsercore.exe is leveraged as a token-accessing helper process.

How this answers your question:

- The question states:
  - There was suspicious WMI process creation.
  - During the same incident, there was a possible attempt to access a Primary Refresh Token (PRT).
  - The answer points to browsercore.exe and asks that this be scrutinized to confirm PRT-related activity.

From the logs we examined (even though they are from 2024-06-20 rather than 2024-07-04), we see a clear, repeated pattern where:

- WMI (WmiPrvSE.exe) is used to spawn PowerShell (suspicious WMI-based process creation).
- That PowerShell runs get-userprttoken.ps1 or similar PRT-stealing scripts.
- Those scripts explicitly:
  - Aim to retrieve a user’s PRT on Azure AD-joined/hybrid machines.
  - Use browsercore.exe as the mechanism for accessing the PRT.
- Browsercore.exe is then:
  - Spawned as a child process of those scripts.
  - Flagged as suspicious and as an IOC by Defender alerts.
  - Tightly correlated in timing with the PRT-theft PowerShell activity and with WMI spawning PowerShell.

Conclusion:

- Yes, browsercore.exe should absolutely be considered suspicious in the context described.
- The telemetry clearly confirms that:
  - browsercore.exe is being invoked by malicious PowerShell scripts designed to steal Primary Refresh Tokens.
  - Those scripts are in turn launched via WMI (WmiPrvSE.exe), matching the “suspicious WMI process creation” behavior.
  - In this environment, browsercore.exe is not just a benign component; it is being weaponized as part of a PRT theft tooling chain.
- Therefore, scrutinizing browsercore.exe around the specified incident time is the correct approach: it is very likely the process directly involved in accessing/attempting to access the PRT as part of that attack.

Thought: We’ve identified various ransomware-related alerts. Now we must pinpoint, for the specific incident about a compromised user dropping get-userprttoken.ps1 (e.g., on vnevado-win11t), which device had the ransomware payload remotely launched, as indicated by the final (“end”) alert. The relevant alert type is “Ransomware payload remotely launched.”, and we need the device name from the alert evidence.

Steps:
1) Identify the incident that includes “Possible compromised user account delivering ransomware-related files” alerts.
2) Within that incident, find all “Ransomware payload remotely launched.” alerts.
3) Determine which of those is the “end alert” (based on EndTime or incident LastActivityTime).
4) Join the corresponding alert to AlertEvidence to get the DeviceName.

To start, I’ll list all security incidents to locate the one containing our compromised user account alerts and related ransomware alerts.

Action: execute[
SELECT 
  TimeGenerated,
  IncidentName,
  Title,
  Severity,
  Status,
  FirstActivityTime,
  LastActivityTime,
  AlertIds
FROM SecurityIncident
ORDER BY TimeGenerated;
]

Thought: We’ve identified multiple “Ransomware payload remotely launched.” alerts, each with a VendorOriginalId that should match AlertEvidence.AlertId. Now I need to:
- Pull all evidence rows for those ransomware-payload alerts from AlertEvidence.
- See which devices they refer to (DeviceName).
- Then determine which one is the relevant “end alert” for the compromised-user incident (likely the one tied into the same broader incident that has the “Possible compromised user account delivering ransomware-related files” alert and the get-userprttoken.ps1 evidence).

First, I’ll query AlertEvidence for any records tied to the “Ransomware payload remotely launched.” alerts by joining SecurityAlert and AlertEvidence on VendorOriginalId = AlertEvidence.AlertId and filtering by DisplayName.

Action: execute[
SELECT 
  sa.SystemAlertId,
  sa.VendorOriginalId,
  sa.StartTime,
  sa.EndTime,
  ae.TimeGenerated AS EvidenceTime,
  ae.DeviceName,
  ae.AccountName,
  ae.AccountUpn,
  ae.FileName,
  ae.ProcessCommandLine
FROM SecurityAlert sa
JOIN AlertEvidence ae
  ON sa.VendorOriginalId = ae.AlertId
WHERE sa.DisplayName LIKE 'Ransomware payload remotely launched%'
ORDER BY sa.EndTime, ae.TimeGenerated;
]

Thought: The previous join between SecurityAlert and AlertEvidence returned no rows because AlertEvidence.AlertId is not equal to SecurityAlert.VendorOriginalId; it appears to be the same GUID with a “da” prefix. For example:
- SecurityAlert.VendorOriginalId: d35af110-f09a-461d-b9eb-dd5ca3808737_1
- AlertEvidence.AlertId:           dad35af110-f09a-461d-b9eb-dd5ca3808737_1

So the correct join key is:
AlertEvidence.AlertId = CONCAT('da', SecurityAlert.VendorOriginalId)

Now I will:
1) Join SecurityAlert and AlertEvidence using this mapping.
2) Filter on DisplayName = 'Ransomware payload remotely launched.' to get all such alerts.
3) Look at the devices involved (DeviceName) and their EndTime to identify which device corresponds to the “end alert” (the latest in the chain for this incident).

Action: execute[
SELECT 
  sa.SystemAlertId,
  sa.VendorOriginalId,
  sa.StartTime,
  sa.EndTime,
  ae.TimeGenerated AS EvidenceTime,
  ae.DeviceName,
  ae.AccountName,
  ae.AccountUpn,
  ae.FileName,
  ae.ProcessCommandLine
FROM SecurityAlert sa
JOIN AlertEvidence ae
  ON ae.AlertId = CONCAT('da', sa.VendorOriginalId)
WHERE sa.DisplayName LIKE 'Ransomware payload remotely launched%'
ORDER BY sa.EndTime DESC, ae.TimeGenerated DESC;
]

Thought: We’ve already pulled all “Ransomware payload remotely launched.” alerts and joined them to their evidence. Now I just need to identify which device appears in the “end alert” (the final ransomware-payload alert in the incident) and report that device name. From the joined results:

- There are four distinct “Ransomware payload remotely launched.” alerts (by SystemAlertId).
- The ones with the latest EndTime (the end of the chain) have EndTime = 2024-06-20 09:34:37.872610+00:00:
  - SystemAlertId 63421576-f354-5bba-974d-2e744ab44577
  - SystemAlertId 89b41efc-e77c-5195-ec98-358dbc7d8200

Looking at their evidence:

- SystemAlertId 63421576-f354-5bba-974d-2e744ab44577 has DeviceName:
  - vnevado-win11t.vnevado.alpineskihouse.co

- SystemAlertId 89b41efc-e77c-5195-ec98-358dbc7d8200 also has DeviceName:
  - vnevado-win11t.vnevado.alpineskihouse.co

Thus, the ransomware payload was remotely launched on the device vnevado-win11t (FQDN vnevado-win11t.vnevado.alpineskihouse.co) according to the final ransomware-payload alerts.

Manatee Tempest overlaps with activity tracked by the cyber intelligence industry as EvilCorp, UNC2165, and Indrik Spider.

question_dict.question: Related to this alert, there was also an incident where file backups were deleted. Can you identify the command used in the process that deleted the file snapshots and shadow copies?
solution: A possible attempt to access Primary Refresh Token (PRT) was detected for the AadUserId `731adb71-b11c-4bbf-850b-57989b350e96`.
File backups, including all snapshots and shadow copies, were deleted using process `7236` at `2024-06-20t09:10:51.2193152z` with the command line `vssblatemp.exe delete shadows /all`.

Action: execute[
SELECT AlertName, Description, SystemAlertId, TimeGenerated
FROM SecurityAlert
WHERE Description LIKE '%ransomware-related%'
   OR Description LIKE '%possibly compromised%'
   OR AlertName LIKE '%ransomware%';
]

Thought: The initial aggregation on AlertEvidence shows many ransomware-related evidences where the account fields are blank, and some associated with concrete accounts like dp5hn. To confidently identify the compromised user that was dropping ransomware-related files across multiple devices, I should:

1) Use AlertEvidence to identify ransomware-related files (by ThreatFamily/Title/Categories/AttackTechniques).
2) Extract file hashes and device names from those evidences.
3) Join those with DeviceFileEvents on hash (e.g., SHA256 or SHA1) and device, to find which InitiatingProcessAccountName/Upn actually created/dropped those files.
4) Count how many distinct devices each account was responsible for; the account with ransomware-related file activity on multiple devices is likely the compromised one.

I’ll perform such a join, focusing on ransomware indicators and counting devices per initiating account.

Action: execute[
SELECT
    d.InitiatingProcessAccountUpn AS account_upn,
    d.InitiatingProcessAccountName AS account_name,
    d.InitiatingProcessAccountDomain AS account_domain,
    COUNT(DISTINCT d.DeviceName) AS affected_devices,
    COUNT(*) AS file_events
FROM DeviceFileEvents d
JOIN AlertEvidence a
    ON (
        (a.SHA256 IS NOT NULL AND a.SHA256 <> '' AND a.SHA256 = d.SHA256)
        OR (a.SHA1 IS NOT NULL AND a.SHA1 <> '' AND a.SHA1 = d.SHA1)
       )
    AND a.DeviceName = d.DeviceName
WHERE
    (a.ThreatFamily LIKE '%ransom%'
     OR a.Title LIKE '%ransom%'
     OR a.Categories LIKE '%ransom%'
     OR a.AttackTechniques LIKE '%ransom%')
    AND (d.InitiatingProcessAccountUpn IS NOT NULL AND d.InitiatingProcessAccountUpn <> ''
         OR d.InitiatingProcessAccountName IS NOT NULL AND d.InitiatingProcessAccountName <> '')
GROUP BY
    d.InitiatingProcessAccountUpn,
    d.InitiatingProcessAccountName,
    d.InitiatingProcessAccountDomain
ORDER BY
    affected_devices DESC,
    file_events DESC
LIMIT 10;
]

A security incident involving ransomware-like behavior impacting several devices has been observed. Initial detection included the use of PsExec to launch a command on a remote device, suggesting lateral movement using this tool. This was followed by suspicious activities leading to compromised assets exhibiting ransomware-like behavior. The attacker might be using the specified user account, IP, or device to infect multiple devices with ransomware. Automated remediation actions were considered to address the threat. What is the name of the file that is associated with the ransomware-like behavior?

I’ll start by listing all tables in the database.

('System recovery setting tampering', 'System recovery setting tampering has been observed on this device. Adversaries might be attempting to delete or remove built-in operating system data and turn off recovery services to prevent recovering a corrupted system. This may deny access to available backups and recovery options.

Operating systems may contain features that can help fix corrupted systems, such as a backup catalog, volume shadow copies, and automatic repair features. Adversaries may stop or delete system recovery features to augment the effects of Data Destruction and Data Encrypted for Impact.

Many native Windows utilities have been used by adversaries to disable or delete system recovery features:
•	 vssblatemp.exe can be used to delete all volume shadow copies on a system using the following command: [vssblatemp.exe delete shadows /all /quiet]

•	wbblatemp.exe can be used to delete the Windows Backup Catalog using the following command: [wbblatemp.exe delete catalog -quiet]

('System recovery setting tampering', 'System recovery setting tampering has been observed on this device. Adversaries might be attempting to delete or remove built-in operating system data and turn off recovery services to prevent recovering a corrupted system. This may deny access to available backups and recovery options.

Operating systems may contain features that can help fix corrupted systems, such as a backup catalog, volume shadow copies, and automatic repair features. Adversaries may stop or delete system recovery features to augment the effects of Data Destruction and Data Encrypted for Impact.

Many native Windows utilities have been used by adversaries to disable or delete system recovery features:
•	 vssblatemp.exe can be used to delete all volume shadow copies on a system using the following command: [vssblatemp.exe delete shadows /all /quiet]
•	Windows Management Instrumentation can be used to delete volume shadow copies using the following command: [wmic shadowcopy delete]
•	wbblatemp.exe can be used to delete the Windows Backup Catalog using the following command: [wbblatemp.exe delete catalog -quiet]

('System recovery setting tampering', 'System recovery setting tampering has been observed on this device. Adversaries might be attempting to delete or remove built-in operating system data and turn off recovery services to prevent recovering a corrupted system. This may deny access to available backups and recovery options.

Operating systems may contain features that can help fix corrupted systems, such as a backup catalog, volume shadow copies, and automatic repair features. Adversaries may stop or delete system recovery features to augment the effects of Data Destruction and Data Encrypted for Impact.

Many native Windows utilities have been used by adversaries to disable or delete system recovery features:
•	 vssblatemp.exe can be used to delete all volume shadow copies on a system using the following command: [vssblatemp.exe delete shadows /all /quiet]

•	wbblatemp.exe can be used to delete the Windows Backup Catalog using the following command: [wbblatemp.exe delete catalog -quiet]

('System recovery setting tampering', 'System recovery setting tampering has been observed on this device. Adversaries might be attempting to delete or remove built-in operating system data and turn off recovery services to prevent recovering a corrupted system. This may deny access to available backups and recovery options.

Operating systems may contain features that can help fix corrupted systems, such as a backup catalog, volume shadow copies, and automatic repair features. Adversaries may stop or delete system recovery features to augment the effects of Data Destruction and Data Encrypted for Impact.

Many native Windows utilities have been used by adversaries to disable or delete system recovery features:
•	 vssblatemp.exe can be used to delete all volume shadow copies on a system using the following command: [vssblatemp.exe delete shadows /all /quiet]
•	Windows Management Instrumentation can be used to delete volume shadow copies using the following command: [wmic shadowcopy delete]
•	wbblatemp.exe can be used to delete the Windows Backup Catalog using the following command: [wbblatemp.exe delete catalog -quiet]
